title: Blonde
text:
Do you know, blonde one, what favor I request

when I cover the altars with offerings?

Not rich furnishings, not proud household gods,

nor a table that flatters appetite.


A district on Aragua's banks

that would provide me simple foods,

where near my rustic homes

a little stream runs among rocks.


To shelter me in summer heat,

I also want a grove

where beside the willow the proud coconut grows.


Happy me if in this shelter I die;

and as I breathe out my fleeing breath,

I seal on your lips the final farewell!
editorial_note: The translation keeps Bello's pastoral wish for a modest refuge and final kiss.

title: First Station
text:
The fever of my arms has already completed a day's march

and the lions of my poetic spirit are still standing:

muscles alert for new claw-strokes

and lungs firm for new roars.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the brief stanza's muscular image of poetic force still ready after labor.

title: They Are Not for the Lyre...
text:
Hands that hate calm are not for the Lyre;

to sing to you I have plucked my soul!

With the tremor of a bride at her beginning,

with the bewilderment of a novice,

the innocence of the pages, a flock of gazelles,

awaits before my eyes the coming of the Canticle,

virgin as the foam of the Atlantic

before the passing of the caravels...
editorial_note: The translation preserves the invocation to song and the untouched Atlantic image before the caravels.

title: Casiquiare
text:
Venezuelan citizen,

Casiquiare is the open hand of the Orinoco

and the Orinoco is the soul of Venezuela,

which gives to the one who does not ask the water it has left over

and to whoever comes to ask it, the water it still has.

Casiquiare is the symbol

of that man of my people

who kept giving everything, and when he was left with nothing

flowed into Death, great as the Ocean.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the river as a civic symbol of generosity that empties itself into death.

title: Informality
text:
I have no notion of time.

My heart is a clock

that from meditating on the hours

fell behind.


Every minute it ponders,

every second it contemplates,

and with that notion of time

one gets nowhere.


I always get everywhere

an hour after

or an hour before,

because my heart, at moments,

stops, to listen to itself.


I have no notion of time,

that is why I often think

that when I die, I will die

after the day of my death...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the comic clock-heart conceit and its final temporal paradox.

title: Silence
text:
When you fall mute,

when I go blind,

we will have our hands

and silence.


When you grow old,

when I grow old,

we will have farewells

and silence.


When you are dead,

when I am dead,

they will have to bury us together

and in silence;


and when you rise again,

when I live anew,

we will love each other again

in silence.


When everything ends

forever in the Universe,

it will be a silence of love,

silence.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the simple parallel movement from bodily loss to cosmic love-silence.

title: April Moon
text:
April moon, low-cut,

with a circumscribed marsh,

naked, with the pure

nakedness of a breast with child.

Full moon, cow's udder,

with little calf star;

how pure the breast becomes

when the child hangs from it!


Tonight I do not feel

nor even a shadow of hatred toward anyone

nor sorrow at seeing myself imprisoned,

nor desire for them to remove

the shackles they put on me.


There is nothing more impure, nothing,

than the breast of women,

but there is nothing purer

nor better to look at

than a breast outside the breast

and a child beside it.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the moon-and-maternal-breast imagery and the prisoner's sudden peace.

title: To Florinda in Winter
text:
To the young man who spoke to you of love

you said yesterday, Florinda, that he should return,

because in your hands you had flowers to spare

to laugh at spring.


Autumn arrived: bed and coverlets

the vine gave you in its shedding of leaves,

and the man who spoke to you of love came,

and again you told him: Wait.


And now you wait, remote vision,

gray countryside, broken fence,

the late shoot now without warmth


that the severed vine left you,

because when love comes in autumn,

if we let it go, it never returns.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the seasonal warning that late love, once dismissed, does not come back.

title: Sonnet of the Poor Rhyme
text:
You give me your bread kneaded in your hand,

you give me your bread baked on your hearth,

you give me your bread ground on your stone,

you give me your bread pounded in your mortar.


You give me your hut wrapped in your palm,

you give me your bed sunk in your corner,

you give me your sip, squeezed from your thirst,

you give me your clothes, sweated in your sweat.


You give me, oh Juan, your beggar's give-me,

you give me, oh Juan, your poor man's take,

your clear faith, your dark shelterlessness,

and I give you, for what by giving I hope,

the dark waiting with which I follow you

and the clear heart with which I love you.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the humble gift-catalog and the deliberately plain poor-rhyme diction.

title: Return to the Sea
text:
It is always the sea where one loves best,

it was always the sea where I loved you best;

love, like the sea, cannot be smoothed by anyone

nor the sea, like love, moderated by anyone.


No one makes us familiar like the sea

nor perseveres like the wave,

nor does the one who says most in what lives and dies

tell us more than the sea tells us.


Let us go again to the sea; I want to find for you

the bluest hour to kiss you

and the farthest place to love you,

where water is at once water and abyss,

on the high sea, where the very air

gives one air to love and another to death.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's sea-love analogy and the final double atmosphere of love and death.
